operations.name: Isidore Begun

expected.charges: Smith Act (18 U.S.C. § 2385)
expected.convicted: No — acquitted by directed verdict, September 30, 1952
expected.sentence: NO SENTENCE. Second period of pretrial custody, after the government invalidated the Civil Rights Congress Bail Fund bonds in July 1951 and Judge Sylvester Ryan ordered the defendants apprehended unless they furnished private replacement bail. Begun was returned to custody in July, was one of four defendants still jailed at the end of the month and one of only two still jailed on August 8, and was released on $10,000 privately furnished bail in mid-August 1951. Neither the return date nor the release date is given in the sources, so the return is recorded to the month only and no release date is entered.

operations.name: Naoichi Seto

expected.name: Naoichi Seto
expected.description:
Naoichi Seto was an Issei Honolulu resident, priest of Tenri Oahu Church and barber shop owner. JCCH records his birth year as 1901. His individual record documents arrest in June 1943, Honolulu Immigration Station detention, Honouliuli July-December 1943, mainland transfer in December 1943, Sharp Park December 1943-January 1944 and Santa Fe January 1944-October 1945. He returned to Hawaii aboard Yarmouth in November 1945. This was administrative US wartime civilian detention in the context of Japanese ancestry. No individual criminal conviction, imposed judicial sentence or exact arrest or release day is established. Source: https://incarceration.jcchawaii.org/internees/seto-naoichi

operations.name: Pierce C. Wetter

expected.charges: Espionage Act of 1917 and/or the Sedition Act of 1918
expected.sentence:
5 years.

ADMITTED TO BAIL, APRIL 2, 1919. The Federal Circuit Court of Appeals ordered thirty-eight of the men convicted in the Chicago mass trial released on bail pending its review of the case; the bonds ran from $5,000 to $10,000, with Haywood alone required to provide $15,000. Fifty-five others convicted in the same case did not seek bail. The order is not the release: each man left Leavenworth when his bond was actually furnished, which for those whose dates are recorded here fell between April 28 and September 28, 1919. Reported in the New York Times and across the wire services, April 3, 1919.

operations.name: Rebecca M. Garrison

expected.name: Rebecca M. Garrison
expected.description:
Rebecca M. Garrison was from Joplin, Missouri. Rebecca M. Garrison was a member of the National Woman’s Party and one of the "Silent Sentinels" imprisoned during the 1917-1919 campaign to picket the Wilson White House for woman suffrage. Her date of death is unresolved. (born June 23, 1892)

She was arrested on February 9, 1919 at the final watchfire demonstration and sentenced to five days in the District Jail; Stevens dates the imprisonment entry to February 10, the day of sentencing. She was released early on February 13.

On the name: this record was filed as “Rebecca Harrison”. The Joplin residence, the February 1919 demonstration and the five-day sentence all correspond to Rebecca M. Garrison, and “Harrison” appears to be a transcription or printing error.
